title: GPIO: General Purpose Pins
description: Every wire on ARIA's chassis ends at a pin. This lesson is a tour of what each kind of pin is actually for.

content.value: GPIO stands for General Purpose Input/Output — a pin that isn't hard-wired to one job. You decide in your program whether a given GPIO pin reads a sensor (input) or drives a motor or LED (output). That flexibility is why one small board can control such different parts.
Not every pin on the board is a GPIO pin, though. A few are permanently reserved for power and ground, and a couple have a special extra ability worth knowing about.

content.title: 📌 Tap a pin
content.hint: Every pin on ARIA's controller falls into one of these four kinds.

pins.label: 3V3
pins.detail: Outputs a steady 3.3V. Use this to power small sensors that need 3.3V, not to power motors — it can't supply much current.

pins.label: GND
pins.detail: Ground — the 0V reference every other pin's voltage is measured against. Every part on the board shares this same ground.

pins.label: GPIO 2
pins.detail: A general-purpose pin, also wired to the board's onboard LED on most dev boards — a handy pin to blink first.

pins.label: GPIO 4
pins.detail: A plain digital pin — set it HIGH or LOW, or read HIGH or LOW from it, your choice in code.

pins.label: GPIO 5
pins.detail: Another general-purpose pin. On ARIA, a pin like this drives one side of the motor driver.

pins.label: GPIO 34 (ADC)
pins.detail: An input-only pin with an analog-to-digital converter — it can read a whole range of voltages, not just HIGH or LOW, which is how ARIA measures her ultrasonic sensor's echo timing indirectly through supporting circuitry.

pins.label: EN
pins.detail: The reset pin. Pulling it low restarts the board, the same as a reset button.

pins.label: VIN
pins.detail: Where external 5V power comes in, separate from the USB port — this is how ARIA's battery powers the board once it's not plugged into a computer.

pins.label: GND
pins.detail: A second ground pin. Boards usually break out several, since almost every part needs one.

pins.label: GPIO 18
pins.detail: A general-purpose pin capable of PWM — you'll use exactly this ability in the next lesson.

content.value:
POWER    supplies a fixed voltage out, or brings external power in
GROUND   the shared 0V reference (Module 3's "ground" idea, on real pins)
GPIO     you decide: input or output, in your program
SPECIAL  a GPIO pin with one extra ability (analog reading, reset, etc.)

When you wire an ultrasonic sensor, an LED and a motor driver onto ARIA, each connection is really a choice: which GPIO pin, configured as input or output, wired to which part. Everything else in this module and the next is about what you can do once that connection exists.

Not all GPIO pins are equal — some are input-only, some can do PWM and some can't. Real boards ship with a pinout diagram exactly like the one above for this reason; check it before wiring, not after something doesn't work.
Key takeaway: GPIO pins are general-purpose — your program decides whether each one reads or writes. Power and ground pins are fixed; a few pins have extra abilities worth knowing about.

quiz.question: What does GPIO stand for, and what does that mean in practice?
options: General Purpose Input/Output — you choose in code whether a pin reads or writes
Ground Pin Input/Output — a pin that's always grounded
General Power Input/Output — a pin only for power
quiz.explain: "General purpose" is the key word — the same physical pin can be an input one project and an output the next, decided entirely in software.

quiz.question: Why can't you use the 3V3 pin to power ARIA's motors?
options: It only supplies a small, steady voltage meant for light loads like small sensors, not the higher current motors draw
3V3 pins don't exist on real boards
Motors can't run on 3.3V ever, on any board
quiz.explain: The 3V3 pin can only supply a limited current. Motors need more current than that, and are powered from the battery through the motor driver instead.

quiz.question: Every part on ARIA's board shares the same ground pin (or pins). Why does that matter, callback to Module 3?
options: It doesn't matter, ground is just decorative
It gives every part the same 0V reference, so voltage readings between parts agree
quiz.explain: Same idea as Module 3's ground lesson — one shared 0V floor is what makes readings from different parts comparable at all.
